subject: Re: [ACME] Post-call: Model fit & evals + function-calling JSON schema check
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>

Subject: Post-call recap + next steps: model fit & evals / function-calling checks

Alex — thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from our discovery and the agreed next steps from Redwood: 

Summary of needs (from call):
- ACME needs high-throughput structured shipping predictions for 200k orders/day ingestion.
- Strict JSON schema compliance for downstream systems (no freeform blobs).
- Low-latency (<200ms p95) inference for interactive correction flows; batch scoring ok for backfill.
- Concern about quality regressions when we update models/quantization settings.

Redwood recommended starting points (based on the workload we talked through):
- redwood-chat-13b (balanced latency / structured output reliability)
- redwood-instruct-70b-quant (for higher quality on complex normalization; consider for nightly batch)
- If you need faster responses with strict cost targets: redwood-7b-quant with KV cache enabled and deterministic prompt recipes.

What we'll run for the initial evaluation:
1) Small-scale model fit eval: run 10k example prompts (you confirmed you can share a sample subset) against the three model variants above.
2) Schema compliance test: validate function-calling / structured output against ACME's shipping JSON schema (please see attached acme_shipping_schema_v1.json).
3) Regression guards: baseline metrics (exact-field-level match, token-level F1, average parsing success) + prompt set tied regression alerts.

Deliverables we'll share:
- acme_eval_report_v1.pdf (sample result summary) — attached
- acme_prompt_sets_v1.json (the prompts & evaluation harness we'll use) — attached + Drive link
- Suggested model configuration and quantization profiles for Dedicated/Private if you decide to move beyond hosted testing

Next steps / asks:
- Please confirm you can share the 10k sample dataset (S3 link or secure Drive) and whether PII must be redacted.
- Confirm a 60–90 minute SE session next week for the schema/function-calling deep-dive (Dev will join).

I'll follow up with an invite after you confirm times.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Account Executive | Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa — this is super helpful. Quick clarifying Qs from our side before we share data:

1) JSON schema enforcement: when you say "schema compliance test", do you run strict validation at generation time (i.e., model must output valid JSON) or do you post-process/repair outputs? We need to avoid manual fixes downstream.
2) Retries / idempotency: if a model returns malformed JSON on a request, what retry strategy do you recommend? We need to be sure retries don't cause duplicates or inconsistent state in our pipeline.
3) How long does the 10k eval typically take and will you provide raw outputs so we can run our own validation?

We can share a 10k sample (anonymized) as a temporary S3 link if that's okay. Priya — looping you since this touches ingestion/ops.

Appreciate the quick turnaround.

—Alex
Alex Johnson | Head of Data Products, ACME Inc.
alex.johnson@acmeinc.com

From: Dev Patel <dev.patel@redwood.ai>

Subject: Re: Post-call recap + next steps: model fit & evals / function-calling checks

Alex — thanks for the questions. Short answers + recommended approach below. Happy to dive deeper in the SE session.

1) Schema enforcement strategy:
- Prefer schema-first function-calling: we register the JSON schema / function signature with the model runtime so the model is guided to emit the expected fields.
- At generation time we perform strict schema validation. If the output fails validation we do NOT silently repair by default — we mark the output as a failure in the eval. For production paths we can enable optional repair with deterministic parsers, but for the eval we'll surface raw failures so you can see failure modes.

2) Retries & idempotency:
- Recommended approach: 1 retry with minimal jitter for transient generation/parsing errors, then surface to downstream for manual or automated repair.
- Add an idempotency token per request (order_id + request_seq) so retries are safe. If you use our Dedicated runtime we can also store a quick write-ahead log of accepted responses to avoid duplicate downstream side effects.
- For batched backfills, rely on batch job dedupe using order_id keys; for interactive flows enforce single-apply semantics on ingestion.

3) Eval mechanics and artifacts:
- 10k prompts: hosted evals against three model variants typically complete within 2–6 hours depending on concurrency knobs; we'll provide raw outputs (ndjson) and parsed results.
- We'll provide a Drive link with: raw_outputs.ndjson, parsed_results.csv, per-field match stats, and the eval harness (python scripts) we used. See link: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/acme/evals/20260318

Attached: acme_shipping_schema_v1.json (schema we'll validate against).

If you want stricter production guarantees we can propose Dedicated capacity with a small reserved pool and autoscaling — that reduces noisy-neighbor variance and gives predictable tail latency.

Happy to review the S3 sample and confirm redaction requirements.

—Dev Patel
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
dev.patel@redwood.ai
